title: Smoked Shrimp Po'Boy
summary: Plump Gulf shrimp kissed with smoke, piled into crisp French bread with spicy remoulade, shredded lettuce, tomato, and pickles. Mississippi Gulf Coast in a sandwich.
story: Gulf shrimp if you can get them — Mississippi shrimpers know what they're doing.

items: 1 1/2 lbs large shrimp, peeled and deveined
2 tbsp olive oil or melted butter

steps.title: Season the shrimp
steps.body: Toss the shrimp with the oil, Cajun seasoning, garlic powder, and paprika. Rest 15 minutes.

steps.title: Smoke
steps.body: Smoke at 225°F for 30–45 minutes, until pink and firm (145°F internal). Don't overcook — shrimp go fast.

steps.title: Make the remoulade
steps.body: Stir the remoulade ingredients together. Chill until serving.

steps.title: Toast the bread
steps.body: Butter the rolls and toast cut-side down in a skillet or on the smoker until golden.

steps.title: Build it
steps.body: Remoulade on both sides, lettuce, tomato, pickles, then a heap of smoked shrimp. More remoulade on top.

proTips.text: Gulf shrimp if you can get them — Mississippi shrimpers know what they're doing.
Shrimp overcook in a blink. Pull them the second they're pink and curled into a C.
Dress it right before serving so the bread stays crisp.
Toasting the bread in butter is not optional.

title: Smoked Whole Duck
finish: 160°F in the breast, 170°F in the thigh
summary: A whole duck, injected and smoked low over fruit wood until the skin turns crisp and golden — with a drip pan of liquid gold underneath.
story: Kelly injects most of his fowl — turkey, duck, all of it. The injection keeps the lean breast juicy while the smoker does its work, and scoring the skin lets the fat render out instead of going rubbery. Finish hot for the crackle. Save every drop of fat from the drip pan; that is liquid gold for potatoes.

steps.title: Inject the bird
steps.body: Whisk the injection ingredients until smooth. Inject all through the breast, thighs, and legs — a little in each spot; do not overfill one place.

steps.title: Score and season
steps.body: Pat the duck completely dry, inside and out. Score the skin in a crosshatch pattern, cutting through the fat but not into the meat. Season all over and inside the cavity. Tuck the orange quarters inside if using.

steps.title: Rest
steps.body: Rest uncovered in the fridge overnight if you can — that is the crispy-skin secret. At least 1 hour if not.

steps.title: Smoke
steps.body: Smoke at 250°F, breast-side up, with a drip pan underneath to catch the fat. Apple or cherry wood. Smoke 3–4 hours until the breast reads 160°F and the thigh reads 170°F.

steps.title: Crisp the skin
steps.body: Crank the pit to 400°F for the last 15–20 minutes for crackling skin.

steps.title: Rest and carve
steps.body: Rest 15–20 minutes before carving so the juices settle.

proTips: Save every drop of fat from the drip pan — duck fat is liquid gold for potatoes.
Do not skip the scoring. That is how the fat renders out instead of staying rubbery.
Fruit wood is the classic pairing for duck.

title: Pepper Jelly Glazed Smoked Oxtails
finish: Meat pulls easily from the bone
summary: Smoke, braise till they surrender, then lacquer in a sweet-heat pepper jelly glaze. Sticky, beefy, and not like anybody else's oxtails.
story: Kelly had never cooked oxtails before this one. Most recipes go Jamaican-style or straight BBQ sauce — this one goes sweet-heat instead. Pepper jelly, a Southern grocery staple, reduces with the braising liquid into a sticky glaze that clings to every piece. Smoke first for the bark, braise till the meat gives up, glaze till it shines.

steps.title: Season
steps.body: Season the oxtails all over. Rest 1 hour, or overnight in the fridge.

steps.title: Smoke
steps.body: Smoke at 250°F over hickory or oak, 3 hours, until the bark sets.

steps.title: Braise
steps.body: Move to a Dutch oven or foil pan with the onion, garlic, and beef broth. Cover tight. Braise at 275°F (smoker or oven) 2½–3 hours, until the meat pulls from the bone.

steps.title: Make the glaze
steps.body: Lift out the oxtails. Strain the braising liquid and skim the fat. Simmer 1 cup of the liquid with the pepper jelly, vinegar, and Worcestershire until thick and sticky.

steps.title: Glaze and serve
steps.body: Toss the oxtails in the glaze until every piece shines. Serve over rice or grits.

proTips: Red pepper jelly gives color; green gives a fresher bite. Both work.
The vinegar keeps the sweetness from going candy — do not skip it.
Make extra glaze. People will ask for it.
These reheat beautifully. Arguably better the next day.

title: Pork Belly Burnt Ends
summary: Meat candy. Barky pork belly cubes braised in butter, brown sugar, and honey, then lacquered in Kelly's Ember Finishing Glaze.
story: Burnt ends started as the barky trimmings Kansas City pitmasters gave away — now they are the bite everybody fights over. Cubed belly takes the same treatment: smoke for bark, braise till the fat renders, then glaze. Kelly finishes his in his own Ember Finishing Glaze, and that sweet-heat lacquer is what makes the pile shine.

items: 1 whole pork belly (8–10 lb), skin removed
1 cup Kelly's Ember Finishing Glaze (or your favorite BBQ sauce)

steps.title: Cube and rub
steps.body: Cut the belly into 1½-inch cubes, keeping them even so they cook alike. Toss in the rub until coated on all sides.

steps.title: Smoke
steps.body: Smoke at 250°F over hickory, 3 hours, until the bark sets and the edges crisp.

steps.title: Braise
steps.body: Move to a foil pan. Scatter the butter over, then the brown sugar and honey. Cover tight with foil. Back on the smoker 1½–2 hours, until probe-tender — the probe slides in like butter.

steps.title: Glaze
steps.body: Drain off most of the liquid. Toss the cubes in Kelly's Ember Finishing Glaze until every piece shines.

steps.title: Tack up
steps.body: Back on the smoker uncovered 15–20 minutes to set the glaze.

proTips: Even cubes matter more than anything. Small ones dry out, big ones stay chewy.
Do not skip the covered braise — that is what renders the fat down.
Go light on the final sauce. They should shine, not swim.

title: Honey Garlic Glaze
finish: Thick enough to coat a spoon
summary: Sweet, savory, sticky — with an Asian lean. Honey, garlic, hoisin, and soy. Goes good on pork, chicken, whatever your taste desires.
story: Kelly wanted a glaze with an Asian lean for pork loin or belly, and asked for hoisin in it. The hoisin brings the deep savory-sweet backbone, the honey brings the shine, and the garlic and ginger do the talking. Brush it on in the last stretch of the cook — it burns fast over direct heat.

items: 1/2 tsp red pepper flakes (optional, for heat)

steps.title: Combine
steps.body: Combine the honey, hoisin, soy sauce, garlic, vinegar, ginger, and pepper flakes in a small saucepan.

steps.title: Simmer
steps.body: Bring to a gentle simmer over medium heat, stirring, 4–5 minutes until the garlic softens and it thickens slightly.

steps.title: Finish
steps.body: Take off the heat and stir in the sesame oil.

steps.title: Use it
steps.body: Brush over pork, chicken, or whatever your taste desires in the last 15–20 minutes of the cook, or toss cubes in it to finish.

proTips: The sesame oil goes in off the heat — it turns bitter if it boils.
This burns fast over direct heat. Last 15–20 minutes only, or use it as a finishing toss.
The hoisin makes it thick enough on its own — no cornstarch needed.
Double it. It disappears.

title: Deer Camp Smoked Venison Stew
summary: A stick-to-your-ribs stew. Seared venison braised low in a Dutch oven on the smoker with root vegetables and tomatoes, so the whole pot picks up that wood flavor.
story: Kelly asked for a venison stew with tomatoes in it — diced from a can, or whole ones quartered up when you've got them. The Dutch oven goes straight on the smoker so the braise drinks in the smoke while the venison goes tender.

items: 2 lbs venison stew meat (shoulder or hindquarter), cut in 1½-inch chunks
1 can (14.5 oz) diced tomatoes, or 3–4 whole tomatoes, quartered

steps.title: Sear
steps.body: Season the venison with salt and pepper. Heat the oil in a Dutch oven over medium-high and sear the meat in batches until browned on all sides. Set aside.

steps.title: Build the base
steps.body: In the same pot, cook the onion until soft, about 5 minutes. Stir in the garlic and tomato paste and cook 1 minute more.

steps.title: Braise
steps.body: Pour in the beef broth and tomatoes, scraping up the browned bits. Stir in the Worcestershire, thyme, and bay leaves. Return the venison to the pot.

steps.title: Smoke
steps.body: Cover and place on the smoker at 275°F for 2 hours.

steps.title: Vegetables
steps.body: Stir in the carrots, potatoes, and celery. Cover and cook 1 to 1½ hours more, until the meat is fork-tender and the vegetables are soft.

steps.title: Serve
steps.body: Fish out the bay leaves, rest 10 minutes, and serve.

proTips: Venison is lean, so don't rush it — if the meat fights the fork, it needs more time, not more heat.
Sear in batches. Crowding the pot steams the meat instead of browning it.
This is even better the next day, once the flavors settle in.

title: Smoked Venison Shepherd's Pie
summary: Ground venison in a savory gravy with peas, carrots, and corn, under a smoked cheddar mashed potato crust. The whole skillet goes on the smoker until the top turns golden.
story: Kelly said this one was made exactly the way he'd make it — no notes. The fork-ridged mash isn't just for looks: those ridges are what turn brown and crispy in the smoke.

items: 2½ lbs russet potatoes, peeled and chunked

steps.title: Brown
steps.body: Brown the venison in a large cast iron skillet over medium-high heat, breaking it up. Drain off any liquid. Season with salt and pepper.

steps.title: Vegetables
steps.body: Add the onion and carrots; cook 5 minutes until softened. Stir in the garlic and tomato paste; cook 1 minute.

steps.title: Gravy
steps.body: Sprinkle in the flour and stir 1 minute. Pour in the broth, scraping the pan. Stir in the Worcestershire and thyme. Simmer 5 minutes until it thickens into a gravy, then fold in the peas and corn. Spread it level.

steps.title: Mash
steps.body: Boil the potatoes until fork-tender, about 15 minutes. Drain, then mash with the butter, milk, salt, and smoked cheddar until smooth.

steps.title: Top
steps.body: Spread the mash over the meat, edge to edge. Rough up the top with a fork so the ridges catch the smoke and crisp.

steps.title: Smoke
steps.body: Place the skillet on the smoker at 375°F for 25–30 minutes, until the top is golden and the edges are bubbling. Rest 10 minutes before serving.

proTips: Those fork ridges aren't just for looks — they're what turn brown and crispy in the smoke.
Drain the venison well after browning so the gravy stays rich, not watery.
A 12-inch cast iron skillet is the perfect vessel — stovetop to smoker, no extra dishes.

title: Smoke and Ember Venison Pot Roast
summary: The Mississippi-style roast, translated for deer and branded our way. Ranch, au jus, a whole stick of butter, and pepperoncini — plus new potatoes, baby carrots, celery, and tomatoes, all braised in one Dutch oven on the smoker.
story: Kelly wanted this one named Smoke and Ember Venison Pot Roast, and he built it like a full one-pot meal: whole new potatoes, baby carrots, celery, and tomatoes go in around the roast so nothing's missing when the lid comes off. The butter does the work the fat would do on a beef chuck, since venison runs lean.

items: 3–4 lb venison roast (hindquarter, neck, or shoulder)
6–8 pepperoncini peppers, plus a splash of the juice
1 can (14.5 oz) diced tomatoes, or 3–4 whole tomatoes, quartered

steps.title: Sear
steps.body: Season the roast generously with salt and pepper. Sear it hard on all sides in a Dutch oven over medium-high heat.

steps.title: Season
steps.body: Sprinkle the ranch seasoning and au jus mix evenly over the roast. Lay the stick of butter right on top. Scatter the pepperoncini around it and add a splash of their juice.

steps.title: Smoke
steps.body: Cover and place on the smoker at 275°F for 2 hours.

steps.title: Vegetables
steps.body: Nestle the potatoes, carrots, celery, and tomatoes around the roast. Cover and cook 1½–2 hours more, until the meat shreds easily and the vegetables are tender.

steps.title: Serve
steps.body: Shred the meat right in the pot, stir everything through the juices, and serve.

proTips: Don't lift the lid to peek — venison dries out fast when the pot loses its steam.
If it fights the fork, give it another 30 minutes, not more heat.
The vegetables go in late on purpose — 4 hours would turn them to mush.

title: Harold's Smoked Venison Summer Sausage
summary: Classic deer-camp sausage. Venison mixed with pork or beef fat for the richness it lacks, seasoned with mustard seed and garlic, then slow-smoked in fibrous casings.
story: Named for Harold Caldwell, one of the three men the venison page is dedicated to. Kelly ran this one by his buddy, who said that's exactly how he does his. The fat can be pork or beef — cook's choice. The curing salt and the overnight rest are non-negotiable: low-temp smoking without cure isn't safe, and the rest is where the tang develops.

items: 2 lbs ground pork or beef fat (the fat the venison's missing)
Fibrous sausage casings, about 2½ inch diameter

steps.title: Mix
steps.body: Mix the venison, pork or beef fat, all the seasonings, and the cold water in a big bowl until it gets sticky and tacky — about 2 minutes of real mixing. That's what binds it.

steps.title: Stuff and rest
steps.body: Stuff into the casings firmly, squeezing out air pockets, and tie the ends. Refrigerate overnight, 12–24 hours, so the cure does its work and the flavors marry.

steps.title: Dry
steps.body: Hang or lay on the smoker at 130°F for 1 hour with no smoke, just to dry the casings.

steps.title: Smoke low
steps.body: Raise to 150°F with smoke for 2 hours.

steps.title: Finish
steps.body: Raise to 175°F and smoke until the internal temp hits 152°F, about 3–4 hours more.

steps.title: Chill
steps.body: Straight into an ice bath for 15 minutes to stop the cooking. Hang at room temp 1 hour to bloom, then refrigerate.

proTips: Don't skip the curing salt and don't skip the overnight rest — low-temp smoking without cure isn't safe.
Mix until tacky. Under-mixed sausage crumbles when you slice it.
The ice bath isn't optional — it stops the cook and keeps the texture snappy.
Make it your own: fold in a cup of diced pepper jack cheese, diced jalapeños, or both — whatever sounds good — right along with the seasonings.

title: Deer Camp Sweet Heat Chili
summary: Not your standard chili. Bush's baked beans bring the sweet, chipotles and hatch chiles bring the smoky heat, and the whole pot rides the smoker over pecan or maple wood.
story: Kelly wanted this one different from the regular chili recipes out there — sweet and spicy, with Bush's baked beans and kidney beans. The hatch chiles were his call, and so was the light wood: pecan or maple, so the smoke stays sweet with the beans.

items: 2 hatch chiles, roasted, peeled, and diced (or 1 can diced hatch chiles)
2 chipotle peppers in adobo, minced, plus 1 Tbsp adobo sauce
1 can (28 oz) Bush's baked beans, undrained
Shredded cheddar, sour cream, and sliced green onions, for serving

steps.title: Brown
steps.body: Brown the venison in a Dutch oven over medium-high heat, breaking it up. Drain off any liquid and season with salt and pepper.

steps.title: Vegetables and spices
steps.body: Add the onion, bell pepper, and hatch chiles; cook 5 minutes until soft. Stir in the garlic, chili powder, smoked paprika, cumin, and oregano; cook 1 minute until fragrant.

steps.title: Beans
steps.body: Stir in the chipotles and adobo sauce, then the baked beans (with their sauce — that's the sweetness), kidney beans, tomatoes, and broth.

steps.title: Smoke
steps.body: Cover and place on the smoker over pecan or maple wood at 275°F for 2–3 hours, stirring once or twice, until thick and rich. (Stovetop works too: simmer 1 hour, partially covered.)

steps.title: Serve
steps.body: Serve with cheddar, sour cream, and green onions.

proTips: Don't drain the baked beans — their sauce is what makes this chili sweet.
The chipotle heat builds as it sits, so go easy if you're serving it straight off the smoker.
Pecan or maple keeps the smoke sweet with the beans — hickory would bully the sweetness.

title: Abby's Lemon Pepper Trout
summary: Simple and clean. The trout goes on the grill skin-down, butter melts over the top, lemon pepper does the rest.
story: Named for Kelly's daughter Abby. Kelly's take on trout: lemon pepper and butter, straight on the grill over a light wood.

items: 4 whole trout (about 10–12 oz each), cleaned, or 8 fillets
Fresh dill or parsley, chopped, for serving

steps.title: Season
steps.body: Pat the trout dry. Rub the outside (or both sides of fillets) with olive oil and season generously with lemon pepper, inside and out.

steps.title: Butter and lemon
steps.body: Stuff a couple lemon slices and a spoonful of butter inside each fish (or lay lemon slices and butter pats over fillets).

steps.title: Grill
steps.body: Grill over indirect heat at 275°F with a light wood — alder or apple — for 25–35 minutes, until the flesh flakes easily and hits 145°F.

steps.title: Serve
steps.body: Shower with fresh dill and serve with the remaining lemon.

proTips: Don't flip it. Skin-down the whole cook keeps the delicate flesh intact and lets the butter baste down through.
Alder or apple keeps the smoke light — heavy woods overpower trout.

title: Megan and David's Smoked Catfish
summary: Southern staple, done right. A simple brine, a Cajun crust, and a mild wood smoke — fillets go on skin-down and never flip.
story: Named for Megan and David. Kelly's rules for catfish: brine it, trim the red meat off wild-caught fillets, and keep the wood mild — pecan, alder, or maple, never hickory.

items: 3 Tbsp Cajun seasoning (store-bought works, or mix: 1 Tbsp paprika, 2 tsp garlic powder, 2 tsp onion powder, 2 tsp salt, 1 tsp black pepper, 1 tsp cayenne, 1 tsp dried thyme)

steps.title: Brine
steps.body: Dissolve the salt and brown sugar in the cold water, add the bay leaves, peppercorns, and lemon, and submerge the fillets for 1–2 hours in the fridge. Rinse and pat dry. Don't go longer than 2 hours — fish gets mushy past that.

steps.title: Trim and season
steps.body: If working with wild-caught catfish, trim the dark red meat off the fillets — that's where the muddy taste lives. Brush with olive oil and coat generously with Cajun seasoning on both sides.

steps.title: Smoke
steps.body: Smoke at 225°F over a mild wood — pecan, alder, or maple — skin-down, for 1½–2 hours, until the fish flakes easily and hits 145°F.

steps.title: Butter and serve
steps.body: Brush with melted butter in the last 15 minutes. Serve with lemon wedges.

proTips: Catfish skin sticks — oil the grates well or lay the fillets on foil with holes poked in it.
Don't flip. The skin side protects the flesh from the heat.
Keep the wood mild — hickory would bully the fish.
